p001.title: Read the passage
p001.text:
The Richter Scale is a way of measuring the magnitude of earthquakes. The scale goes from one to ten. We
often can’t feel earthquakes below five. Anything above seven is likely to cause serious damage. The worst
earthquake on record was in Alaska in 1964. It reached 9.2 on the scale. Most earthquakes go unnoticed,
although the National Earthquake Information Center (NEIC) in Colorado records over fifty every day.

p002.title: Read the story
p002.text:
Scorpions are among the oldest creatures on earth and scientists think they might have been one of the
first to crawl out of the sea and start living on land. They look like small lobsters, but their tails are different.
The scorpion’s tail has a fat bulge called a telson which contains its venom and a sharp stinger to stab its
prey. There are 1200 species of scorpion worldwide, but only 90 live in the United States. The Arizona bark
scorpion is the only one that is potentially fatal.

p003.title: Read the story
p003.text:
The Apache were not one single tribe, but a group of them: the Western Apache, Chiricahua, Jicarillo, Kiowa,
Lipan, and Mescalero. They lived in the Southern Great Plains of Texas, Arizona, New Mexico, and
Oklahoma. They had semi-permanent homes called wikiups (or wigwams) made from living trees domed
over to make a roof that was then covered in bark and grasses. They also had portable homes tike tents:
Teepes were made from long poles covered with a cone of hides sewn together. They could quickly be set
up or dismantled and carried on sledges or horse-drawn wagons.

p004.title: Read the passage
p004.text:
Scientists deal in facts. They have a question and they set out to find the answers. Sometimes
they find them by observation of the natural world. Sometimes they find answers by doing
experiments. They then analyze the data, which is all the evidence collected together, and draw
conclusions from it. Sometimes they find an answer to the question; sometimes they just find
more questions!

p005.title: Read the story
p005.text:
We are surrounded by systems. There is a school system which organizes education. There isa
legal system which looks after laws and rights. There is a political system for our government. In
our bodies we have a circulatory system and a nervous system. A system is a set of connected
things working together and there are many examples in the natural world.

p006.title: Read the story
p006.text:
Rubber is a great natural material. Unfortunately, unless it has other ingredients added to it, it is
of little use. Natural rubber breaks into pieces if it freezes, and dissolves into a gooey mess if it
gets too hot. The man who discovered how to make rubber stable spent many years
experimenting. His name was Charles Goodyear and he wanted to make rubber strong enough to
make car tires that would last, and keep drivers and passengers safe.

p007.title: Read the passage
p007.text:
People first began to live in settlements thousands of years ago. Over time, some settlements
grew into villages with more permanent houses. Some were in places that made it easy to trade
with other villages. They became prosperous and grew into towns. People in towns began to
specialize in different jobs and group together to provide public buildings for government and
religion. Some towns became bigger and more important and became cities. Now every country
has many cities, like New York or San Francisco, and one capital city, such as Washington D.C.,
where the government is located.

p008.title: Read the story
p008.text:
Years ago, food didn’t travel very far, and many people grew their own vegetables. Finding a
caterpillar in a cabbage or a beetle in your broccoli wasn’t unusual. However, things have changed,
and that includes the way we farm. Farms are much larger than they used to be, and they are
heavily mechanized. Fields can artificially receive just the right amount of water and nutrients and
can be sprayed with pesticides to kill insects. The advantages are less labor, fewer damaged crops,
and higher crop yields.

p009.text:

they are well camouflaged and blend in with the plants they inhabit ______ {

p010.title: Read the passage
p010.text:
Herculaneum was a Roman town on the coast of Italy. It was destroyed when Mount Vesuvius, a volcano,
erupted in 79 CE. As the volcano erupted, is poured volcanic mud through the streets and buildings of the
town at such a pace that people couldn't escape. In time, it set like plaster, preserving many objects people
used in their daily lives, such as wooden beds, pottery lamps, and bowls of food. Archaeologists have
carefully excavated the buildings. Underneath the volcanic material they found mosaics and beautiful wall
paintings. From all the remains, they have been able to build up a picture of what life in a Roman city would
have been like 2,000 years ago.

p011.title: Read the story
p011.text:
In 2003, a group of naturalists on a mountainside in Tanzania, Africa, discovered a new kind of monkey. It
is one of thousands of new species discovered by scientists every year. Fortunately, organizations like the
World Wildlife Fund are around to help save such animals. The kipunji is three feet tall and has a thick coat
of grey-brown fur. Its face is black and it has side whiskers that make it look like a Victorian gentleman.
There are thought to be around 1,000 of them living in Tanzania’s mountains alone.

p012.title: Read the story
p012.text:
Fish are aquatic animals and have been around for 500 million years. They have fins to help them move
through the water, and gills which allow them to breathe. The gills extract oxygen from water. Most fish
have skeletons made of bones (just like we do), although some—such as sharks—have skeletons made of
cartilage, which is a softer, more flexible material. (The tip of your nose is supported by cartilage rather
than bone, which is why it moves.) The majority of fish are cold-blooded, which means they don’t regulate
their own body temperature like we do (we sweat to cool down and shiver to warm up), but match the
temperature of their surroundings. There are around 25,000 species of fish that we know about: some no
bigger than your little fingernail, others up to forty feet long.

p013.title: Read the text
p013.text:
Diamante poems are diamond-shaped. They have just seven lines and the first and last lines contain a single
noun each. Line four has nouns, too, but there are four of them. Lines two and six contain only a pair of
adjectives, The remaining lines comprise three verbs or gerunds each. If the opening and closing nouns are
synonyms of each other, the poem is a synonym diamante, and if the opening and closing lines contain
words which are opposites, then it is an antonym diamante. While some types of poem, such as sonnets,
are very old—Shakespeare wrote his more than 400 years ago—diamante poems are relatively new. They
were invented in 1969 by an American poet called Iris McClellan Tiedt and are now very popular in schools.

p014.title: Read the passage
p014.text:
We think of deserts as hot, dry, and full of sand. Some deserts are like that, of course, but deserts
are Classified by geologists according to the amount of rain they get: below 250mm a year. Some
deserts, like the Atacama in Chile, get no rain at all. Plants and animals rely on dew and the
moisture from fog. Others, like the Arabian Desert in Oman get almost a whole year’s rain in a few
really heavy downpours, which leads to dangerous flooding. There are ancient deserts like the
Namibian Desert in Africa with majestic, multi-colored sand-dunes, and there are flat deserts like
the Gibson Desert in Australia, which is covered in dry grass. Temperatures can reach over 50°C.
On the other hand, there are deserts like the Gobi in Mongolia where the temperature remains
below freezing for six months or the year, and the largest desert in the world is Antarctica, which
is an area of 5,500 square miles of ice and snow.

p015.title: Read the story
p015.text:
Great white sharks have a fearsome reputation. They have 250 very sharp teeth. These are used
to tear their food into chunks the shark can swallow whole. They can reach over 20 feet in length
and can swim at 15 miles an hour. In comparison, a really fast swimmer can reach a top speed of
just 6 miles per hour—no match for a great white. However, they prefer to eat seals, and that’s
the reason why there are more shark attacks on humans in places where seals live: they mistake
swimmers for seals. Great whites are pale underneath and dark on top to avoid detection when
they hunt. From under the water, they blend in to the light from above.

p016.title: Read the story
p016.text:
The word quilt comes from the Latin word culcita, meaning a stuffed mattress or cushion. In the
1800s, quilting became very popular in America. It was a way to make something useful from
scraps of fabric too small for anything else. However, the technique of sandwiching padding
between layers of material and fixing it in place with decorative stitches wasn’t originally to make
comforters or bed covers, but to make clothing. It is impossible to tell when people began quilting,
but 5,000 year-old evidence was found recently in the Temple of Osiris at A by dos in Egypt. In the
Medieval Period (476-1453) armor and chainmail was rough and cold, so soldiers wore quilted
clothing underneath to protect their skin. In the days of Queen Elizabeth I of England (1533-1603),
it became very fashionable for men to wear jackets stitched from “doubled” padded cloth which
became known as doublets.

p018.title: Read the passage
p018.text:
The Taj Mahal in India is one of the most famous buildings in the world. It is made from white
marble and has a beautiful dome. In front of it there is a long pond, and on calm days, as the sun
sets, the entire facade is reflected in its calm waters. It is visited by millions of people a year and
is considered one of the most romantic places in the world. In fact, the Taj Mahal is a tomb, built
by a prince hundreds of years ago to honor of his beloved wife.

p019.title: Read the passage
p019.text:
Why do flamingoes stand on one leg? One idea is that it gives one foot at a
time a chance to dry out. Another idea is that they keep warm if they tuck
one foot up out of the water. A third theory is that when they stand on one
leg, to a shrimp swimming about under the water, they look more like a plant.
In fact, the real reason is to save energy. By shifting their weight to one side,
they can rest without using muscles to maintain their balance.

p020.title: Read the story
p020.text:
In April 2024 there will be a rare eclipse visible from the United States. It will be a total eclipse,
leaving the U.S. in darkness for about 4 minutes. The next one will not happen until 2045. Total
eclipses happen because the Earth wobbles on its axis. That means that sometimes the Moon is
closer to the Earth. Being closer, it looks bigger from Earth and so it covers the Sun completely.
For most eclipses the Moon only partially covers the Sun, leaving a ring of light all around. These
are called annular eclipses.

p021.title: Read the passage
p021.text:
Remarkably, cats only meow when they talk to their humans—not when they talk to each other. With
other cats, they might growl, hiss, spit or yowl. Overall, however, most cat communication is through
body language, especially use of the tails. A cat that is relaxed will stroll about with its tail up in the air. A
very happy cat might even curl its tail backward towards its head. If the cat’s fur is standing on end and
the tail looks like a bottle brush, then it is threatened or angry. If the cat’s tail is swishing rapidly back
and forth it is usually very cross. On the other hand, a gently swishing tail suggests the cat is
concentrating.

p022.title: Read the story
p022.text:
Fossils need the right conditions. There are all kinds, from fossils of algae that sank to the sea floor a
billion years ago to whole dinosaurs that fell into a lake 60 million years ago. To become a fossil, there has
to be water and sediment. Sediment is fine soil, sand or clay particles. The plant or animal sinks to the
bottom of a body of water and is covered by layer upon layer of sediment. The soft tissues disolve until
only a skeleton is left. In due course, the layers of sediment solidify into stone that often becomes
exposed. Ground water eventually dissolves the bone, leaving a shape—like a jelly mold—inside. Over
time, water rich with minerals fills up the mold and it hardens into the shape of the original bone. After
even more time, the top layers of the rock wear away because of wind and rain and the fossil bone lies
exposed, ready for a paleontologist to find.

p023.title: Read the text
p023.text:
In the past, long-distance travel was only possible by sea, and navigators were welcomed home with
bonfires. Soon, port cities began constructing stone platforms on which to build their bonfires, and later,
stone platforms. The higher the platform, the further out to sea it could be seen, helping guide ships into
safe water. In time, the platforms became towers with huge hearths in open galleries at the top: our first
lighthouses. Nowadays lighthouses warn ships of danger. Each one has a unique combination of light
colors and signals so that mariners know exactly where they are. If they can see the light flashing, they are
Sailing into danger. At one time, there were over a thousand lighthouses in America alone, but with
modern navigational aids, some have been put up for sale and many are being turned into holiday homes.

p024.title: Read the passage
p024.text:
Trees are like icebergs. Much of their mass is hidden under the surface of the ground. What we
see above ground are the trunk and the canopy. The canopy is the umbrella of branches and leaves
that gives the tree its shape. What we can’t see is the complex network of roots without which a
tree couldn’t survive. Trees are not like carrots: they don’t usually have a single main or “tap”
root, but a whole host of roots. The small, thin roots near the surface collect water and nutrients
from the ground to feed the tree, while the thicker, deeper roots act as an anchor to keep the tree
steady. Most people think that the radius of the roots is the same as the radius of the tree canopy,
but they'd be wrong. Roots can grow three times as wide as their canopy in the first few years,
but after that, roots grow outward for as many meters as the tree is high.

p025.title: Read the story
p025.text:
[A] In 1621 the Dutch West India Company decided to colonize America from Cape Cod to the
Delmarva Peninsula. [B ] The company was interested in the fur trade and wanted Dutch people
to settle in America so they could help ship the animal skins back to Europe. It took around 30
years for New Netherlands to get started, but by the middle of the seventeeth century, the
settlements had expanded. The capital of New Amsterdam was located on the tip of Manhattan
island. It was a bustling port with a large fort to protect ships and a busy town were all kinds of
European goods could be found. [C] In 1664, however, the Dutch handed the city over to the King
Charles Il of England, and it was named a fer the king’s brother, the Duke of York.

p026.title: Read the story
p026.text:
Having hiccups can be annoying and they can take a while to stop, but they are rarely harmful.
Remedies include drinking a glass of water, putting an ice-cube or cold spoon down the back of
your neck, breathing into a brown paper bag, holding your breath, or having somebody jump out
at you, shouting “boo!” Usually, however, they just go away on their own after a few minutes.
They are caused when the diaphragm misbehaves. The diaphragm is a large muscle curved like a
mushroom. When you breathe in, your lungs push it flat. When you breath out, the diaphragm
returns to its dome shape and pushes the air out again. Eating or drinking too fast, or getting very
excited or upset, can make the diaphragm flatten when it should be dome-shaped and dome up
when it should be flat, at odds with your breathing. The body makes you hiccup to get the two
back in sync.

p027.title: Read the passage
p027.text:
Graphene is an amazing form of carbon. Carbon has many different forms, from the burnt bits on
your morning toast to a sparkling diamond. What makes graphene unique is that it is the only 2D
material we know about. It is just one atom thick. You would need three million graphene sheets
to make a stack just one millimeter high. It is incredibly strong, and can stop a bullet better than
steel, but it is also flexible and can conduct electricity. With such a remarkable material, we may
soon have computer screens that can be scrunched into a pocket like a paper hanky!

p028.title: Read the story
p028.text:
Sea spiders can be found at the bottom of the ocean all around the world. They aren’t spiders at
all but may have evolved from the same ancestor many millions of years ago. They have thin,
spindly legs and tiny bodies and come in all shapes and sizes. Some are about the size of your little
finger, but others, especially those deep in chilly Arctic waters can grow to incredible sizes of up
to two feet across. They mainly feed on sponges and sea anemones, although they don’t kill them:
they suck nutrients from them. The strangest thing about sea spiders is that they breathe through
their legs, which are porous and can extract oxygen from sea water.

p029.title: Read the story
p029.text:
Audiobooks are now outselling e-books, even though they are dearer than printed books and much
more expensive than e-books. There are millions of titles available. When the first e-books
appeared, publishers feared they would no longer be able to afford to commission new books.
That has all changed. People live very busy lives these days, and whereas in the past you had to
do your chores before you could settle down with a great story, now you can do both together.
With an audio book you can walk or jog, garden or do chores, or entertain yourself on a long
journey. And experts now believe that listeners get more out of an audio book than they do from
the printed page.

p030.title: Read the passage
p030.text:
Brad and Stacey exchanged glances and backed out to the edge of the crowd. Stacey took hold of
Brad’s hand. Tempers were running high, and by the look on the faces of the mill workers by the
gates and the farmers bunched up in the road, there was going to be trouble.

p031.title: Read the poem
p031.text:
Claws click, chalk crumbles,
Wings widen, a tussock tumbles
Down, down, down. It falls as if
There is no end to this towering cliff
Where stands the beast, noble-limbed,
Eyes agleam, and head to the wind.
A flick of his tail and breathing fire
He takes to the air and soars ever higher.

p032.title: Read the story
p032.text:
Skyler heard the town clock strike eight times and jerked upright. Confused for a moment, he sank
back down onto the pillows and waited. Presently, he sat up again, puzzled. He couldn’t hear any
cars out on the street. What day was it?

p033.title: Read the story
p033.text:
Marsha clutched the flute in her hand and shuffled onto the stage. Her hands shook. She could
hear murmurs and rustling from out front, but there were lights in her eyes and she couldn’t see.
She felt sick. She wanted to run, but the shame! She heard the voice of Uncle Ivan in her head.
“The music wants to play, little Marsha. Just let it.” She took a deep breath, closed her eyes, and
let go.

p035.title: Read the passage
p035.text:
Aria’s mom stared at the spreading pool of maple syrup on the newly mopped floor. A tendril oozed
towards the stove. Aria slid the other two bottles onto the counter and braced for impact. Juggling
with maple syrup bottles? Really? She risked a glance up, but her mom turned without a word,
leaving the screen door swinging noiselessly behind her.

p037.title: Read the passage
p037.text:
A ball of tumbleweed rolled across the concrete. The wind was hot. In the dusty window of the
store was a sign in English and Spanish: Monday-Friday 8-8, Saturdays 8-2. Kepple glanced at the
digital display on his watch: 14:02. They sure were strict on tardiness in this town, he thought
bitterly, giving the locked door handle a savage rattle.

p038.title: Read the poem
p038.text:
Said the Wind to the Moon, "I will blow you out.
You stare
In the air
Like a ghost in a chair,
Always looking what I am about;
I hate to be watched—|I will blow you out."
The Wind blew hard, and out went the Moon.
So deep,
On a heap
Of clouds, to sleep,
Down lay the Wind, and slumbered soon—
Muttering low, "I've done for that Moon."

p039.title: Read the story
p039.text:
The rocks ahead looked like sharks’ teeth snapping at the impossibly blue sky. The air was so clear
JD felt like he could reach out and touch the patches of purple-shadowed snow under the peak.
They were still around a mile distant. The wind whispered encouragement, silvering the short
grass as he squared his shoulders and went on.

p040.title: Read the passage
p040.text:
Peri sat on the boulder and dug her toes deep into the sand. Sunlight fell like a benediction
onto her freckled, upturned face. The sound of the waves was soothing, and the ceaseless
cry of the gulls reminded her of every holiday she’d ever had. Somehow, without the gulls,
it would have been less real.

p041.title: Read the poem
p041.text:
Red faced, gap-toothed, grinning
Candle-lit eyes twinkle at night.
Along the street, children come dinning
Laughing and jostling, feigning fright.
From the fields by the ton
Then never more seen
Now that October’s done
And we’ve had Halloween.

p042.title: Read the passage
p042.text:
Gift wrapped in sunshine, Abby thought, staring out at the new world. The ribbon—almost
a bow—was formed of the twin tire tracks from Mr. Henty’s car. He’d called on his way up
to the Henderson’s saying school was canceled. The old school bus was trapped in Edensville
at the bottom of the long climb and wouldn’t be going anywhere until the big snowplow had
been through.

p043.title: Read the poem
p043.text:
Upon my back, I carry a pack,
A great canvas sack with buckle and strap
Filled to the top with I don’t know what—
Pens and erasers, a book about lasers
Some pencils and paper and homework for later.
Along sidewalk and road, I transport my load,
But am! a mule?
No. Just a child off to school.

p044.title: Read the story
p044.text:
Duh-duh-duh-shwump. Duh-duh-duh-shwump. Jake sits on the wall, rolling his skateboard
back and forth on the uneven concrete. Duh-duh-duh-shwump. One of his sneakers has a
tear along the side and the laces are uneven. Duh-duh-duh-shwump. He thrusts lean legs
out to their fullest extent and then swings them back, slamming the board into the wall. Duh-
duh-duh-shwump. His sudden movement startles me. “So?” he demanded. “Are we going
or what?”

p045.title: Read the passage
p045.text:
People think Mount Rushmore is pretty cool—and it is, but it isn’t as cool as old Blackeyes.
Blackeyes was a “phenomenon,” so Pa always said: a phenomenon of Nature. Blackeyes
was part of the cliff at Eagle’s Ridge. The ground was the kind of rock that made caves.
Soft rock, that broke and shattered. Nature had arranged the pieces like LEGOs, building a
chin here and a nose there, wide cheeks and a broad forehead, so—with two old caves for
eyes—when viewed from the right spot it looked like old Chief Yellowtail that we all called
Blackeyes.

p046.title: Read the poem
p046.text:

p047.title: Read the passage
p047.text:
Above the streets of New York, another world is opened up, full of interesting objects. The
cars of the elevated railway sweep by the upper stories of the houses, but never too fast that
you can’t catch a glimpse into the high-rise lives as they pass by. From here, the view reveals
the secrets of a thousand homes never dreamed of by the giddy, restless crowd that hurries
along impatiently in the streets below.

p048.title: Read the poem
p048.text:
White sheep, white sheep,
On a blue hill,
When the wind stops,
You all stand still.
When the wind blows,
You walk away slow.
White sheep, white sheep,
Where do you go?

p049.title: Read the story
p049.text:
He lived somewhere on the outskirts of town. They said his family was no good, but nobody
knew them, really. He was six years old when I first saw him. He was thin and had a white
face, with blue shadows round his eyes. He sat on the old tree next to the old railroad track
in a t-shirt three sizes too big, playing with a stick—his only toy. Then he began to follow the
tracks, jumping from sleeper to sleeper, trailing the stick along the metal tracks. It had been
a side branch to a mine that had closed when my grandpa was a boy.

knew I was at the edge of panic. Mrs. Williams would be furious when she got back and found
Ghost gone. I had looked everywhere for her. I knew she couldn’t have gotten out, but all her
usual hiding places were empty. On cold days she would head for the basement and the boiler. If
there were strangers in the house, she’d hide under the bed. Most often, she would be curled up

p051.title: Read the poem
p051.text:
In our little boat to glide
On the water blue and wide,
While the sky is smooth and bright,
What could give us more delight?
See the ripples, how they run,
Twinkling brightly in the sun;
While reflected we can see
Shadows of each hill and tree.
See the lilies, round and large,
Floating near the reedy marge,
See the great green dragonfly,
And the swallow skimming by.
See the fishes spring and gleam,
Ere they splash into the stream,
These are all around our boat
On the water whilst we float.

p052.title: Read the story
p052.text:
lt started with a wind that blew in ugly gusts from every quarter of the compass. The wind took
delight in snatching people’s hats from their heads, and rushed maliciously around corners, taking
away the breath of anyone silly enough to be coming the other way. It raced through alleyways
and over gardens, tearing leaves from the neatly trimmed hedges and rattling windows in their
frames. It sent vicious fingers through coats and shoes and went roaring away, first to the woods
above the town, now down to the harbor where the fishing boats strained urgently at their
moorings. Old Sam Corcoran glanced at the advancing line of dark, bubbling clouds still far away
on the mercury-colored horizon, shook his head, and stumped back to his cottage where he
slammed the door and built up the fire.

p053.title: Read the story
p053.text:
He could feel his heart thumping in his chest, just as the guitar case bumped against his back.
‘Don’t let me be late. Don’t let me be late,’ he repeated over and over in his head, the rhythm of
the words beating a tattoo in time with his labored breathing. 43 street. Two blocks to go. He
splashed through a puddle, one part of his mind aware of the cold squelch of his right shoe, the
other focused on the green crossing sign. “Stay green. Stay green. Stay green,’ he thought, hurtling
between a woman with a pushchair who was talking to an old guy with a walking frame. He heard
the woman’s indignant cry as he shot across the road and reached the safety of the sidewalk an
instant before the roar of traffic drowned whatever remark she had made.

p054.title: Read the poem
p054.text:
Silver, black, silver, black,
Chrome and tiles and “mind the gap.”
A rush of air, a burst of light
Strangers’ faces fly from sight.

p055.title: Read the passage
p055.text:
The voices of the children have died away into silence. The artisan has dropped his tools, the artist
has laid aside his brush, the sculptor his chisel. The teeming life of the streets has vanished. Night
has spread her wings over the scene.

p056.title: Read the poem
p056.text:
The cataract strong
Then plunges along,
Striking and raging,
As if a war waging
Its caverns and rocks among;
Rising and leaping,
Sinking and creeping,
Swelling and sweeping,
Showering and springing,
Flying and flinging,
Writhing and ringing,
Eddying and whisking,
Spouting and frisking,
Turning and twisting,
Around and around
With endless rebound;
Smiting and fighting,
A sight to delight in;
Confounding, astounding,
Dizzying, and deafening the ear with its sound.

p057.title: Read the passage
p057.text:
The day was warm and sunny. The eaves dripped musically, and the icicles dropping from the roof
fell occasionally with pleasant crash. The snow grew slushy, but by afternoon recess, as the boys
were playing in their shirt-sleeves, a great cloud began to rise in the west and north—a vast, salty-
blue, seamless dome with edges of silvery light. In fifteen minutes, the wind from the south
ceased. There was a moment of breathless pause, and then, borne on the wings of the north wind,
the streaming clouds of soft, large flakes of snow drove in a level line over the homeward-bound
students. By the time they reached home, the wind was a gale, and the snow a vast blinding cloud,
filling the air and hiding the road.

p058.text:
am waiting for a muse, (Or so my teacher says),
Although I think her views (At least on certain days)
Are not at all like mine, and nor are all her ways.
She said that there are nine (Though I think there are only three),
And they surely won’t have time to come and visit me.
They're to help me write a poem, although how, I cannot see.
I have a pen and notebook, but the time is ticking by.
(It’s awkward when you’re stuck, but know you have to try.)
You end up drawing doodles—of fish—(I don’t know why).
Yet maybe the muses play a game and Miss was actually right,
Because all at once the words just came as though my pen took flight,
And a poem landed on the page: “The Muse Just Out of Sight”.

p059.text:
ease forward, sliding along the ledge, first in shadow, then in the hot sunlight. Ten feet away, the
untidy bundle of twigs sits on the grey granite. A grey feather is plucked from the tender lining
and sails down, down, down, dizzying in its descent. Forward again, hands outstretched. But no
blue speckled egg waits for me. Instead a fluff of feathers, yellow beaked and fierce eyed, defies
me with its look.

p060.title: Read the passage
p060.text:
The board trembles under my feet. The water, turquoise, shimmers in the sunlight filtering
through the high windows. It seems a long way down. Pale faces turn upward to stare. A
bluebottle rams its head stupidly against the dusty glass. If I do this properly, I could get into the
state finals. Slowly, I edge forward until my toes curl over the edge of the platform and raise my
arms above my head.

p061.title: Read the poem
p061.text:
A hand eases along the sand
Beneath the sea,
It spreads questing arms
Towards the rocks,
Terracotta tentacles
In search of home.
A seaside decoration
Lies upon the shore.
It didn’t come from the sky
But from the ocean
Torn from its coral home
By the savage tide.

p062.title: Read the passage
p062.text:
It was growing dark as they neared the lake. They'd been delayed waiting for the park rangers to
arrive and take Julio back down to civilization. Or what passed for civilization—a dozen cabins for
hire to the hunting fraternity and a single, part-time general store. Elliot felt bad that one of the
party would spend the weekend in the hospital with a broken ankle, but he was glad the trip hadn’t
been canceled. The final stretch up to the cabin was a slog done in moonlight, each of the boys a
darker shadow against the forest, but it was a moonlight full of grins.

p063.title: Read the poem
p063.text:
The world has lost her blues
Her yellows and reds and rainbows
For the palette of the moon
In white and silver glows.
My bed is striped in steely bars
From the shining window panes
And there’s black and white and pewter
And frosty silken skeins
Touched now and then with amber
From passing motor cars
Whose lights add golden highlights
Like tiny mobile stars.

p064.title: Read the story
p064.text:
Some people have no curiosity at all. My sister Cory was like that. She couldn’t draw a verbal
picture of what someone looked like or what kind of person they were. She’d been home
the whole day, but when I asked her about the new neighbors, my questions neither
interested nor puzzled her. They were called Latimer, they had lived in Port Royal, the mom
was a teacher, the dad was some kind of federal agent and there was a son called Radson.
What more could I possibly want to know?

p065.title: Read the passage
p065.text:
We pause at the top of the slope, looking across the park. Sol rolls back and forth, one foot on the
ground, gripping the handlebars. BJ squints, assessing the path. A lady and her dog head into the
trees on the right. A mom and two kids play on the swings way over on the left. Clear. I glance at
them and we exchange a nod. Then, with a whoop, we’re off, pedaling faster and faster, grins
plastered to our faces by the wind, hair tugged into tangles. Legs straight out, I keep free of the
whirring pedals as we hurtle down the hill at breakneck speed, and oh, the glory of it!

p066.title: Read the poem
p066.text:
Where I go, he follows me
One step ahead, or two or three,
Sometimes to the right or left is he,
But all the day long, he’s after me.
Sometimes he seems as tall as can be
But he’s terribly thin and more agile than me,
Hiding behind clouds when I stop to see
If he’s under the bench or behind a tree.
He has his own bike and he’s quite carefree
Dashing about in the sun like a bee
And even at night when we’ve eaten our tea
While the lights are on, he’s following me.
He’s a strange companion, fit as a flea
And only at noon and in darkness are we
Apart from each other, I and he
Me and the one who’s following me.

p067.title: Read the passage
p067.text:
The train we had to take left at 4 a.m., and Mom had us up two hours before as we lived so far
from the station... so far from anywhere. It was a still, summer night. The world seemed wrapped
in a comforter of silence and darkness. There was a sliver of a moon above the pines like the rind
of a white squash. It wasn’t enough to dim the stars which spread so thickly in places it looked like
someone had smeared white cotton candy against a black tablecloth.

p068.title: Read the poem
p068.text:
Yesterday is far away,
Its joys and sorrows fled
Tomorrow’s fears may not appear:
We cannot see ahead.
The only thing we have is NOW
We can only shape today.
So make the present all you can
Make, hay, make hay, make hay.

p069.title: Read the story
p069.text:
With Jones and Ellis alongside, I galloped rapidly through the rank grasses toward the base of the
hills. From one of their openings descended a deep ravine, widening as it spilled out on the prairie.
Entering, dirt flying in a choking cloud, we were at once surrounded by stark red-stone buttes. Half
of their bulbous edges were bare; the rest were sparsely populated by dry grass and spiky, uncouth
plants that oozed white sap and malice.

p070.title: Read the passage
p070.text:
Tecumseh woke early. The stillness of the night clung to the sloping walls of the teepee. Stillness,
but not silence. Insects creaked and chattered in the darkness. A log on the fire in the center of
the camp popped and a burned log subsided. Somewhere up on the high plains a wolf howled, and
a wildcat yowled in anger or frustration. He sat up, remembering. What a gathering! The hypnotic
rhythm of the traditional chants... Lalawatheeka’s mysterious songs and the intricate patterns of
dancing feet. They were sleeping now. Now was his chance to live up to his name: panther
crossing. Silently, Tecumseh took his spear from beneath his bedroll, slipped on his moccasins and
slid noiselessly into the silver promise of dawn.

p071.title: Read the passage
p071.text:
Jack scowled over his shoulder. “Come on!” he hissed. Three pale faces stared back at him, picked
out in brilliant moonlight. Jack rolled his eyes. “City kids,” he muttered.
The three cousins hunched their shoulders, the nighttime sounds wholly unfamiliar. They kept
close, wondering that what had seemed such a good idea this morning seemed madness at night.
What if Uncle Colly found out? Five more minutes of anxious shuffling through dry grass and over
tree roots close behind Jack, and then they were there, faced with a tall brick wall pierced by a
large, arched doorway. It was ajar. Wordlessly, Jack wormed his way through the narrow gap,
gesturing urgently for them to follow. They had no choice.

p072.title: Read the passage
p072.text:
The sun beat down on the sidewalk, sending up shimmering ripples of air. Heat pooled on the
black top, lakes of heat as far as the eye could see. Brad stepped from one paving slab to another,
avoiding the cracks. He’d always avoided the cracks. When he was little Jed had told him if you
stepped on a crack the devil would come out and grab you, but that was just plain silly. Mind, that
was before Jed had disappeared. What was it now? Two months? Nobody had seen or heard of
him since that day in May when he’d slammed his skateboard into Mayor Denton’s prized Buick
and there’d been a terrible row.

p073.title: Read the poem
p073.text:
A lonely kind of iceberg, softened by the blue,
A regiment of soldiers, swiftly marching through,
Streamers from a mare’s tail, a thunderhead or two,
Millions of pictures up there, but none of them like you.

p074.title: Read the passage
p074.text:
Rollers shoulder their way shoreward, throwing up surfers and seaweed. In the shallows the water
boils like milk towards the wreck of yesterday’s tide: brown-green wrack, plastic bottles, a flip flop,
pieces of other people’s lives. Turbo noses into the piles, sniffs a piece of tarred rope and moves on,
urging me to follow. I obey.

p075.title: Read the poem
p075.text:
with all its different moods
the wind is like a child
first gentle as a feather
then gusting loud and wild
one moment tossing blossom
gently on the breeze
next a ravening hurricane
uprooting homes and trees
and like a child asleep
at night the wind will cease
and until the sun comes up

p076.title: Read the passage
p076.text:
The sightless windows were dark, and the paint was peeling. Baz tried the doorknob. It turned,
but the door seemed stuck. He leaned against it and shoved. Pieces of paint, green with cherry-
red, blue, and black beneath, flaked off and stuck to his sweater. The door yielded reluctantly, and
he had to give it several hard jerks before it opened wide enough for him to squeeze through.
Inside, his sneakers left a trail of damp footprints across the dusty floor.

p078.title: Read the story
p078.text:
Agatha glared at the trolley full of books and stuck her tongue out at Miss Martin’s retreating back.
It wasn’t her fault that she’d misunderstood what she had to talk about in class. As far as she was
concerned the “Big Mac” was a tasty hamburger, not some stupid play by Shakespeare. So that’s
why she was here in the library after school tasked with putting all that day’s borrowed books in
the right places.

p079.title: Read the passage
p079.text:
The sidewalks gasped under the relentless sun. Office blocks threw daggers of light across broiling
air and the city sank into breathless torpor. Nothing moved. The stray cats and mongrel dogs had
found somewhere cool and dark to lie up for the day. There were few pedestrians in this part of
the neighborhood, and even the sleek corporate cars seem to stop coming, waiting for the scant
relief of dusk.

p080.title: Read the poem
p080.text:
The car bumps over a crossing
Jerking me awake
More awake.
It is dark now.
There are trees
Dark wisps that flash past, striping the night.
Now and again there’s a lighted window,
And a figure inside.
Who lives there?
Who are they?
What are they doing?
Do they know I touched them with my eyes
Just once
For a moment
As the car sped by?

p081.title: Read the passage
p081.text:
The boiler gave a last asthmatic sputter, gurgled one last time, and lapsed into silence. Dust motes
sparked through the empty air as the last packing case was taken away. Floorboards creaked,
settling into their worn, familiar shapes. The door closed for the last time, the key turned, and the
empty windows stood, looking blankly out into the sunlit street. Fora moment, the old house was
inclined to despair, but it remembered the shiny new “For Sale” sign outside. Soon new people
would come, and it would stop being just a house and become a home again.

p082.title: Read the poem
p082.text:
Push everything away.
Each person, or sound
All the worries
Complaints...
Everything.
Pull apart from the world
Empty it of voices
All of them
Chattering
Endlessly.
Pay attention to your heart
Enjoy the stillness
Accept dreams
Cherish
Everyone

p083.title: Read the story
p083.text:
Riding the bus on the same route, day after day, is an odd mixture of variety and sameness. I pass
the same shops, the same green-shuttered house at the corner of Wilson and 9", the same car lot
with its perpetual “Sale Now On” sign. Yet the woman with the pushchair waiting at the crossing
is different today than yesterday’s grandfather bending over a stick, and the silver Toyota that pulls
alongside at the railroad crossing is different to the black SUV that was waiting there the day
before.

p084.title: Read the passage
p084.text:
love riding the El, although you can’t see much of the crowded sidewalks of the city. It is simply a
rush of the same people—hurrying this way or that on the same errands, doing the same shopping
or eating at the same restaurants. It is a kaleidoscope with infinite combinations but the same
effects. You see it today, and it is the same as yesterday. Occasionally in the multitude you hit upon
something different, or an odd detail, but the general effect is one of sameness.

p085.title: Read the poem
p085.text:
It gleams.
Colors glint in the light from the lamp.
Gold winks on an edge.
Am I the first to open this treasure box?
It is small... a few inches wide.
Held in one hand, it weighs little
For all the gems it holds.
And around me, others.
Row upon row
Shelf upon shelf
Of treasure-boxes.
Waiting.

p086.title: Read the passage
p086.text:
Millie stood, one hand clutching Mopsie, her disreputable rabbit, the other to her face, where
she resolutely stuck her thumb in her mouth. She twirled from side to side, watching me defiantly.
I glared back at her.
“Mom said,” I began and then sighed. Millie, being Millie, that tactic wasn’t going to work.
Mules weren’t in it. “Oh well,” I said, deliberately nonchalant. “It’s up to you.” I turned and went
back inside, letting the screen door close behind me, and leaving her standing on the patchy grass
at the bottom of the porch steps.

p087.title: Read the poem
p087.text:
One: drape.
It hangs limp, like the scarf Mom wears on Sundays.
Two: a loose knot.
It lies uncertainly, neither one thing nor another, questioning.
Three: bring the fat end across the front and through the middle.
It writhes like an unruly serpent, confused by the mirror.
It squirms first left and right, hands not obeying.
Four: push the end through the front. It’s called a half Windsor.
I wonder what happened to the other half.
It looked easy when Dad did it.

p088.title: Read the story
p088.text:
There was a solid thump. I felt the impact up my arm to my shoulder, but paid it no attention.
My eyes were on the ball. It flew, up, up, up—a speck of dark against the empty blue sky. The
crowd seemed to hush and then I was slammed back to reality with coach yelling at me to run.
Run! First base.... Second... I could already see fielders running backwards, hands outstretched,
eyes on the soaring ball. Third base... But amidst the roar of the crowd I heard the slam of
leather on leather. With every ounce of strength I had, I launched myself at the home plate,
feeling dirt scraping the skin from my arms as I slid the last few feet.

p089.title: Read the acrostic poem
p089.text:
A pool of beans and a dab
Of ketchup from the jar
Fried egg, bacon and sausage
With a cup of tea
When it is still dark
No time—|I need to be off
Then an idea
Fast, no fuss:
Toast.

p090.title: Read the passage
p090.text:
In every neighborhood of New York you can find bodegas. There are ten thousand of them.
The name is Spanish and means store-room. The first bodega-owners were Hispanic and
they opened up small convenience stores in the 1930s and 1940s to supply goods to fellow
immigrants. Nowadays bodegas sell everything from candy and soda to laundry detergent
and shampoo. Some of them include a deli counter or even a coffee counter, and they are
usually open 24/7. This makes them especially useful for shift workers who may have to
pick up a snack at 4 am in the morning while the rest of us are asleep.

p091.title: Read the poem
p091.text:
Across the lonely beach we flit,
One little sandpiper and I,
And fast I gather, bit by bit,
The scattered driftwood, bleached and dry.
The wild waves reach their hands for it,
The wild wind raves, the tide runs high,
As up and down the beach we flit,
One little sandpiper and I.
— Celia Thaxter

p092.title: Read the passage
p092.text:
Not today, thought Emily, staring out across the restless waves. That was the problem with
living in a lighthouse. The sea was heaving up and down like some great sea monster was
shaking out its duvet the way Mom did on laundry day. It rose up in lumps and disappeared
into hollows, and now and again a mad seagull dove into the water and rose into the pencilly
sky with an aluminum foil fish in its mouth. Tuesday. Freya and Sam would probably be at
the mall today, she mused. Was there a word "pencilly"? There should be, because the sky
had the same color as when you rubbed a pencil over and over on the same piece of paper.

p093.title: Read the passage
p093.text:
Woad is a blue dye used to color cloth. Nowadays factories often use synthetic dyes, but
woad is a natural dye and comes from a plant. It has been used for millennia, and samples
have been found in 10" century Viking shops and in Egyptian tombs 4,000 years old. Woad
plants were introduced into the United States by settlers in Plymouth in the early 1600s.
Dyer’s Woad (/satis tinctoria) reached the west coast in the 1850s but has now spread all
over America and become a nuisance.

p094.title: Read the passage
p094.text:
Trees loomed up out of white nothingness. They appeared like sentries on duty and
vanished when I turned to look back. Sabre nudged my leg, and then took a few paces
forward, his black muzzle close to the well-trodden path through the woods that led to
the creek. His tail plumed grey as he turned to look back at me. Then he went back to
the trail, coat flecked with damp. We are the only two out here. I came to restore my
grandpa’s old cabin, and to maybe detect for any gold left behind. They said the claim
had been worked out before my dad was born, but who knows?

p095.title: Read the passage
p095.text:
In our solar system, all the planets orbit the Sun, which is a star. There are billions of stars
in our galaxy. Around 2,500 of them have their own planets, which are known as
exoplanets. NASA is studying them because there may be a few that are just like Earth and
could be habitable. They need to be close enough to their sun that any water doesn’t
freeze, but not so close that any life there would fry. An exoplanet with just the right
conditions is called a “Goldilocks” planet because it is not too hot, and not too cold, but
just right. So far, NASA has discovered seventeen of them.

p096.title: Read the passage
p096.text:
Ganan rested the paddle across his knees and let the canoe drift into the shade of the great
boughs that overhung the riverbank. It was hot today; so hot metal burned. The sky wasn’t
even breathing. No leaves stirred and it was utterly silent, as though even the insects were
faint with heat. The canoe lay balanced, like a bead of mercury on a glass slide, the same
above as below.

p098.title: Read the passage
p098.text:
They caught up with me in the 7" Precinct. It’s harder to slip between realities when
people are firing at you, but it’s the only way to survive. Think of it this way. When you
read a book, you get to the end of the page and then turn over and read the words on
the other side. You don’t see all the pages in between, because you only exist in one
reality: we exist in all of them. Time doesn’t mean much to us, or else it means
everything. You have it as the fourth dimension, but it isn’t. Where your scientists went
wrong is in believing that time only moves in one direction.

p099.title: Read the passage
p099.text:
Trees can live a long, long time. Bristlecone pines are among the oldest individual trees
growing anywhere in the world. One, called Methuselah, growing in the White Mountains
of In yo County, California, has been dated to more than 4,800 years old, which means it
had been growing for 300 years before the pyramids were built! However, there are clonal
trees which are even older. Those are trees which are connected by roots, and although
the trees that push up from underground may only be a few hundred years old, the colony
itself can survive for thousands of years. One colony of quaking aspens in Utah has been
going for 80,000 years.

p102.text:
Violet, frowning, eased off the lid of the box. The cardboard was speckled with age and
some of the blue color had worn off on one corner. She pursed her lips. The attic was very
untidy. Inside was another box, this time in blue velvet, and not very large. It about
covered the palm of her hand, but no more. She turned it over, trying to figure out how it
opened. She gave a sigh. After a few moments fiddling, she found a small, brass button
which popped a catch. A silent “oh” escaped her. She’d been looking for grandpa’s medals
for show-and-tell the week before Veterans Day, but what lay inside was most definitely
not a medal.

p103.title: Read the passage
p103.text:
The Internet has made it easier for people who live far from schools or libraries to get
information. In many ways it has made the world a more equal place—at least for those
that speak English (half the world’s websites are in that language) and who can access it
(just under half the world can’t). But the speed of Internet access can vary enormously—
not only from area to area but from country to country. In a recent report, produced
through a collaborative effort between a British data analysis firm and America’s M-Lab, it
was revealed that the United States, home of the Internet, was 20" when it came to
broadband speed, averaging 25.86 megabits per second. Countries like Lithuania, Taiwan,
and Denmark were much faster, and Singapore, heading list, enjoys an average speed of
60.39.

p104.title: Read the poem
p104.text:
We are glorious precious things
And fly on silent, secret wings
Upon a clear but hidden track,
Going forward—never back.
We are small, but we stop—never!
For nothing, no one, nothing—ever.
Chasing seconds, speeding on,
Pursued by hours we soon are gone.
Use well each cohort, sixty-strong
And you'll have hours of time to use.
Waste us, squander us, all day long
And years of time you’ll surely lose.

p105.title: Read the passage
p105.text:
The island took our breaths away. It lay in the bay like a serpentine pebble, green with
specks of red, set in a sparking sea of silver and aquamarine. There were two hills. The one
to the east was the higher of the two and was crowned by a squat round tower. Tom
thought it had been a lighthouse, but I thought it was probably a windmill. On the mainland
there are many of them: round, whitewashed, with spindly arms creaking slowly, grinding
nothing but air.

p106.title: Read the passage
p106.text:
There is a genus of plants called Tillandsia that grows in places like the West Indies and
South America. In the U.S. you might see examples in California, Louisiana, or Texas.
They’re generally quite small and come in many varieties (there are over 600 kinds), but
what makes them unusual is that they don’t grow in water or soil, but in the air. They are
known as epiphytes from the Greek words epi (above or on) phyte (plant), but they don’t
just grow on other plants, but on rocks, fences, and even telegraph wires. They don’t
damage their hosts like parasites, but simply use them as a surface on which to grow.
Instead, they take moisture and nutrients from the air and the dirt around them.

p107.title: Read the passage
p107.text:
Would she come? Loretta closed her eyes and crossed her fingers under the long pink scarf
that wound twice around her neck. Mina would feel the cold. Muscat to Missoula was
quite a change. Would she even recognize her? Mina had been her best friend right
through to third grade, and Mom and Mina’s mom had been friends too. Mina’s father was
from Oman and he’d had to return there for work. That had been almost two years ago,
and even though they’d texted for the first few weeks, after that they’d lost touch. Then,
last week, out of the blue, Mom received a phone call from Mina’s mom asking if she could
meet them at the airport.

p108.title: Read the passage
p108.text:
To the east the sky looked bruised: all purples and blues with a hint of yellow on the horizon. For
what seemed an age, they watched, too much in awe of the storm to even fear it. They had
reached the wooden cabin at the edge of the gully as the first, fat drops of rain fell. Now it was
as if a fire hose had been turned on the scant shelter. There was a miniature waterfall in one
corner where the tin roof had peeled back from the rafters. The door had long since gone.
“Better than nothing,” Ethan concluded, squatting on his haunches and peering out at the rain.
Aria was gazing out of the empty window frame at the back. “Maybe,” she said cautiously.
“Maybe not.” Then, pointing, “Do you think this thing floats?”

was standing by the hall of mirrors watching the cotton candy guy doing a great trade. It
was then that I had this really strong feeling of... I suppose you’d call it unreality, as though
I was an avatar in a video game, and nothing was really real. All the carnival people looked
the same. They had the same wide-eyed, wide-mouthed smiles, but there was no
expression in them, as though they were fashion store dummies. I began to look into the
faces of the crowds, too, and started noticing that their eyes were empty. That’s when I

p110.title: Read the passage
p110.text:
Some kids collect Pokémon cards, others collect Legos. Some prefer collecting Squishies or
stamps. Saul Dancowicz collects rocks. He’s a self-confessed rock hound. That’s the
nickname for those who scour the countryside looking for different kinds of rocks. He has
samples from all over the world. Many he collected himself, but others, with the help of
his dad, he swapped via a collecting forum. It helps that his dad is a geologist, of course,
but he has several books on rocks, and frequently turns to the Internet. “There’s a great
site called geology.com with pictures to help identify rocks. It’s a great hobby because
there are rocks everywhere, and they’re free.”

p111.title: Read the poem
p111.text:
Sunlight sparkles
Upon impossibility:
Rolling blue,
Frightening power,

Winslow Homer is one of the most famous American painters, best remembered for his
seascapes. He started his career as an illustrator, providing images for sheet-music covers
and magazines, although he didn’t enjoy it much. He was a war correspondent for a time,
but painting pictures of the soldiers made him sad. After that, he painted pictures of
people enjoying the seaside and the countryside of New England. He mostly taught himself
to paint, although he did study in Paris for a short time. His style changed after he visited
the United Kingdom. He stayed in a fishing village in the north of England and was
impressed by the courage of the sailors. He painted the hardship in their wives’ faces and
the fury of the sea. From that point on—wherever he went—he always painted the sea.

p116.title: Read the passage
p116.text:
Igneous rocks are the hardest, strongest rocks on Earth. They are made from magma, or
molten rock. When it solidifies under the ground, it does so slowly, and large crystals form
as the rock cools. That gives us rocks like granite, found in places like Indiana and
Wisconsin, where there are big quarries for building stone. When the molten rock solidifies
above the ground, it cools much more quickly, so the crystals inside the rock are much
smaller. That gives us basalt, found in Washington and Oregon and the most common
bedrock all over the world. If it cools super-fast, it forms a kind of natural glass called
obsidian found in places like Nevada and New Mexico and used by native peoples to make
very fine, very sharp tools.

reach the ocean a hundred kilometers away; equally convinced that if I did get there,
there’d be nobody to witness it. The rocks seemed to stare at me, pressing in with a kind
of timeless malevolence, willing me to be gone.

p119.title: Read the passage
p119.text:
There are 210 species of orchids in the United States, many endangered, but they
represent a tiny fraction of the 25,000 kinds found worldwide, mostly in the tropics. The
majority grow from a pseudobulb: a ball of plant material containing food and water from
which the leaves and the stem of the orchid grow. These pseudobulbs can range in size
from monsters 2.5 meters across to a miniscule 2 mm. Their diversity doesn’t end there.
Some are parasitic and need the support of other plants to survive, while others are
independent. Some have thick, fleshy leaves to conserve water; others have no leaves at
all. One thing they do have in common, however, is their flowers. No matter what their
color, each one is symmetrical, with its right side a mirror image of its left.

p120.text:
When the teacher gets cross, and her blue eye gets black,
And the pencil comes down on the desk with a whack,
We children all sit up straight in a line,
As if we had rulers instead of a spine,
And it's scary to cough, and it’s not safe to grin,
When the teacher gets cross, and her smile goes in.
When the teacher is happy, her smile is so bright,
That the tables get straight, and the reading is right.
The plus and the minus come trooping along,
And the figures add up and stop being wrong,
And we children would like (but dare not) to shout,
When the teacher is happy, and her smile comes out.

p121.title: Read the passage
p121.text:
The United Nations says there are about 7 billion people in the world. It also says that
around 6 billion people have or use a mobile phone. Mobile phones are game-changers.
With them we can access information from anywhere at any time. They help us find our
way to the best shops by GPS or suggest the latest movie to watch. We can even share
pictures instantly with friends. In developing countries, they are even more significant.
They offer access to education, health care information, and news that in the past simply
wouldn’t have been available. It is no wonder that developing countries have adopted
mobile technology up to twice as fast as countries like the United Kingdom and United
States.

Ella felt sweat begin to prickle on her forehead and down her back. Inside the laundry cart
was dark and stifling, the smell sour. She heard the woman close the bedroom door, and
felt the cart bounce along the floor through the large living room towards the door of the
suite. There was a bump as the cart negotiated the do or frame. Ella held her breath. She
expected a challenge, a demand to check the cart’s contents. Then she heard the door click
closed and the crockery trolley ahead begin to rattle down the corridor. Was it that easy?
she wondered as they halted. She felt as though she were floating. Freedom! She pulled
the sheet away from her face, gulping fresh air.

p123.title: Read the passage
p123.text:
There are many famous fast-food restaurants, but have you ever wondered how they got
their names? McDonald’s is easy enough. It was named after Richard and Maurice
McDonald, the brothers who started the burger empire in San Bernardino, California. That
was also home to the first Taco Bell, and although its logo is a picture of a bell, it, too, was
named after its owner, Glen Bell—and its main product, of course. KFC is just an abbreviation
of what the company sells: fried chicken, Kentucky style. But what about Subway? It isn’t
named after an underground railroad, but after the submarine-shaped rolls used to make
sandwiches. It started out as Pete’s Submarines, but because that sounded like “pizza
marines” on a radio commercial, the name was eventually changed to “Subway” in 1968.
